chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 461 to 470, Peyanar's mullai decade of the friend's reassurance (தோழி வற்புறுத்த பத்து): with the rains beginning, the friend tells the waiting wife not to grieve, discredits the konrai that flowered too early, explains the delay by spoil from the enemy, cites the king's release and his own haste, calls her out to see the rightward-rising cloud, and finally rests the guarantee on her own beauty.

461.reading: The friend tells the heroine that the rains have begun, the pidavam buds made lovely by the spray of massed clouds and the forest taking on the drizzle, so she must not grieve: the men in the war camp of the victorious king will not rest content having left her.

thinai_evidence.note: the onset of the rains and the pidavam in bud fix the mullai season of waiting

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தோழி வற்புறுத்த பத்து) names the friend strengthening the waiting wife's resolve; she answers the wife's grief (இனையல்) at the rains' coming

461.nuance: The friend names the absent men only by their place, the camp of a victorious king (வெற்றி வேந்தன் பாசறை): the comfort is that a winning war ends, so the season and the campaign close together.

462.reading: The friend asks the girl why she still weeps on seeing the foolish konrai, which took a stray shower for the rains and put out its garlands: those who crossed the woodland of opening buds are not men to let her beauty fade.

thinai_evidence.note: the konrai of the rainy woodland is the sign in dispute

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தோழி வற்புறுத்த பத்து) names the friend strengthening the waiting wife's resolve; she answers the wife's weeping (கலிழ்வே) at the flowering konrai

462.nuance: The friend does not deny that the konrai has flowered; she denies that the flowering is evidence, calling the tree பேதை, simple, for mistaking an unseasonal shower (ஏதில பெய்ம்மழை) for the true rains. The promise is saved by discrediting the sign.

463.reading: The friend says their lovers will surely come to string the fragrant flowers of the bushes, made lovely by the season, into her fine hair; they have only stayed on to bring back the rich treasure that falls to them from the enemies' land.

thinai_evidence.note: the men are delayed and the friend promises their return

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தோழி வற்புறுத்த பத்து) names the friend strengthening the waiting wife's resolve; she explains the men's delay

463.nuance: The delay is given an honourable cause, the spoil of the enemies' land (நேரார் நாடுபடு நன்கலம்), and the return is pictured as an act of adornment, the man dressing her hair. தொடரி may be the thodari shrub whose flowers he will bring, or 'having strung'; the sense of the line turns on which.

464.reading: The friend says that in the cold season, when the karuvilai opens like eyes and the climbing peerkku vine flowers like gold on the dark bushes, the men who ache to embrace her fine shoulders will not forget the time.

thinai_evidence.note: the blue karuvilai and the yellow peerkku of the mullai hedges

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தோழி வற்புறுத்த பத்து) names the friend strengthening the waiting wife's resolve; she names the season the men cannot forget

464.nuance: The two similes run backwards from the usual: the flowers are likened to an eye and to gold, the very things the waiting woman's eyes and pallor are elsewhere likened to, so the hedge in bloom already shows her face.

465.reading: The friend promises that he will come, driving his tall chariot, swift as falling water, through the rain-made forest so that she may embrace his chest with its tangled flowers; the war-loving chief's enmity has cooled.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest the rains have made is the mullai land and season

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தோழி வற்புறுத்த பத்து) names the friend strengthening the waiting wife's resolve; she announces the end of the war and his coming

465.nuance: The last line gives the reason after the promise: the return depends on the chief's anger being spent (தணிந்தனன் பகையே), so the lover's time is the king's time.

466.reading: The friend tells the sweet-spoken girl with the bright brow that the man has done the great work the king sent him on and the king of the tall-tusked elephant has let him go, so she is sure he will come within the counted days.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend's certainty of the return inside the reckoned days

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தோழி வற்புறுத்த பத்து) names the friend strengthening the waiting wife's resolve; she declares her own certainty (தெளிந்திசின் யானே)

466.nuance: The friend's comfort is not the season but news: the task is done and the king has released him, so she reasons from the court's business to the date. 'Counted days' (எண்ணிய நாள்) implies the wife has been reckoning them.

467.reading: The friend begs the girl not to waste away grieving again and again till her ornaments slip: they say the king of fierce-horned elephants, victorious in war, thinking that those who went on his work have been gone too long, hurries more than they do themselves.

thinai_evidence.note: grief at the man's delay, answered with reassurance

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தோழி வற்புறுத்த பத்து) names the friend strengthening the waiting wife's resolve; she answers the wife's wasting (புனைஇழை நெகிழச் சாஅய்)

467.nuance: The comfort is reported (என்ப, they say) and puts the king on the waiting women's side: he is more eager than we are. The friend borrows the court's urgency to quiet the house's.

comparisons.tenor: the lover's embrace for her shoulders

468.reading: The friend says that the rains have begun this morning, striped frogs croaking and toads swarming, and that today their lover will drive here in his tall chariot with its well-made bells, to be a full feast for her even-jointed, bamboo-full shoulders.

thinai_evidence.note: the frogs' croaking marks the first rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தோழி வற்புறுத்த பத்து) names the friend strengthening the waiting wife's resolve; she announces his coming today

468.nuance: The image of the lover as a guest's feast for her shoulders turns the wife into the host and the returning husband into a guest, the mullai wife's virtue of hospitality applied to her own reunion.

469.reading: The friend calls the flower-eyed girl to come and look: the sky has begun to rain, rising on the right with thunder that shakes the wide heavens, to bring the lord of the hard country where the red quail steal the green millet set out to dry.

thinai_evidence.note: the hard upland country and the first rain

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தோழி வற்புறுத்த பத்து) names the friend strengthening the waiting wife's resolve; she invites the wife to see the rain

469.nuance: The rain does not merely mark the season; it rises on the right (வலன்ஏர்ப்பு), the auspicious side, in order to bring him (தரீஇய), so the friend presents the cloud as the man's escort and its rightward rising as an omen.

470.reading: The friend asks the bright-jewelled girl whether, even if her lover forgot her, her dark-gold beauty, shining in its excellence, would let him forget her in this cold-dew season when the wind blows every night chilling the wide earth with hard dew.

thinai_evidence.note: the cold dew season after the rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தோழி வற்புறுத்த பத்து) names the friend strengthening the waiting wife's resolve; she argues that the wife's own beauty will recall him

470.nuance: The friend concedes the worst case (உள்ளார் காதலர் ஆயின், if he does not think of us) and moves the guarantee from the man's memory to the woman's beauty: it will not let him forget.

links.note: In both, the friend tells the waiting woman that the konrai bloomed foolishly, taking an unseasonal shower for the rains (Natrinai: கார் என்று அயர்ந்த ... மடவ; Ainkurunuru: காரென மயங்கிய பேதையம் கொன்றை).
links.teaches: Natrinai answers a question about the promised date by blaming both the mindless cloud and the flowers, while Ainkurunuru answers tears by blaming only the konrai and then vouching for the man, so the 'foolish flower' was a stock rebuttal the friend could aim at the calendar or at grief.

links.note: Kuruntokai's heroine herself refuses to believe the forest's konrai that says the rains have come, because he does not lie; Ainkurunuru's friend calls the same konrai deceived.
links.teaches: Read together, the two show that discrediting the konrai's sign was the shared way to keep the man's promise unbroken, whether the heroine did it out of trust in his word or the friend did it to stop her weeping.

links.note: Akananuru 364's heroine says the rains have begun and her lover in the fierce king's great camp, set on victory, does not think of them (நம்மும் உள்ளார்); Ainkurunuru 461's friend says the men of the victorious king's camp will not rest content having left her.
links.teaches: The same facts, the rains begun and the man held in a victorious king's camp, support despair in the heroine's mouth and assurance in the friend's, so the mullai situation was fixed and only the speaker decided its meaning.

links.note: Both open on striped frogs croaking and close the scene with the formula கார்தொடங் கின்றே காலை.
links.teaches: The identical formula leads in Akananuru to an evening the heroine cannot swim through and in Ainkurunuru to a chariot arriving today, showing that the first-rain formula was a neutral hinge onto which either the dread of evening or the promise of return could be fastened.

links.note: In Akananuru 164 the hero in camp says his wife could regain her beauty this season if only the fierce king would release him; in Ainkurunuru 467 the friend says the king is hurrying more than they are.
links.teaches: The hero's own speech shows the king as what holds him back, while the friend at home claims the king is more eager than the wives, so the friend's comfort is revealed as persuasion built on a report the camp itself contradicts.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 20's hero says the king's work is finished and the roads are pleasant; Ainkurunuru 466's friend says the king has released him after the great work and she is sure of his coming.
links.teaches: The hero announces the release as a fact on the road, while the friend can only infer it at home and stake her certainty on it, so the release from the king's work was the one event both ends of the mullai separation waited on.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 12's friend takes the dark clouds rising on the right (ஏரும் வலம்) every day as a sign beyond doubt of his coming; Ainkurunuru 469's cloud rises on the right (வலன்ஏர்ப்பு) to bring him.
links.teaches: Kar Narpathu treats the rightward rising cloud as evidence to be read, Ainkurunuru as an escort that brings the man and an occasion to go out and watch, so the omen of the right side could serve the friend both as proof and as a reason to act.

links.note: Both say the rain-season flowers have opened like eyes (கண்ணெனக் கருவிளை மலர; கண்மலர்போற் பூத்தன) as the friend's season sign.
links.teaches: In Kar Narpathu the eye-like flowers speak and announce the man's return, in Ainkurunuru they only mark a season he cannot forget, so the same flower simile let the friend present the hedge either as a messenger or as a calendar.

source_issues: 462 lines 1 and 5 and 465 lines 1 and 2 are repaired readings from tamilvu.org (U. V. Swaminatha Aiyar), agreeing with sangamtamil.com.
468 line 4 (வடி மணி நெடுந்தேர் கடைஇ) is missing from the base text and supplied from sangamtamil.com.
463 line 1: தொடரி may be the plant (thodari) or the verb 'having strung'; the reading is marked uncertain.
